assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance in the sense I value most: magic-wavelength trapping cancels light shifts, and thousands of atoms interrogated at once reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This opens redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and searches for dark matter. The path from idea to working instrument is clearly demonstrated.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and led the early Sr demonstrations; Ye's group brought the systems to the 1e-18 regime and linked them to frequency combs and many-body/spin-physics effects. The two-name credit is compact and defensible. Whether Hall/Hansch-style comb work or ion-clock groups also deserve a share is a question of overlap with earlier prizes rather than of this credit list.
assessment.maturity: Mature: multiple independent labs (Japan, US, Europe, China) operate lattice clocks at comparable accuracy, intercomparisons exist, and an international roadmap toward redefinition is underway. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 (combs) and 2012 (ion control) prizes could lead some members to want a narrower framing.
Formal SI redefinition has not yet happened, which some may consider a reason to wait.
Credit for the original lattice-clock idea versus the later accuracy record may be debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gives inertial sensors, gravimeters, gradiometers and tests of the equivalence principle and of G, whose sensitivity scales with the area enclosed. It is a quintessential measurement technology, and I know from experience how hard it is to make these devices stable in the field.
assessment.attribution: Bordé provided the theoretical framework and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer; Pritchard realized the first atom interferometers with nanostructure gratings and light; Kasevich (with Chu, who is not on this list and already holds a 1997 prize) developed the light-pulse inertial sensors. A fair three-way split is plausible, but the missing Chu-Kasevich link is a complication.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the lab and in the field (gravimeters, commercial devices, 10-metre fountains), but the fundamental-physics payoffs (gravitational waves, dark matter) are not yet realized. Timely but not urgent.
uncertainties: Chu's absence from the credited names makes the Kasevich attribution less clear.
Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 prizes on cooling and BEC.
Competing priority claims for the earliest atom interferometer (Carnal/Mlynek and Keith et al. also in 1991).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a field in which correlated insulators and superconductivity appear in a tunable, clean platform and inspired a large new family of moiré materials. The impact on condensed matter is high and rapidly expanding. As an experimentalist I appreciate how the devices turn a purely theoretical flat-band prediction into a controllable knob.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle in 2011; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the devices and observed correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018. Andrei's early STM and transport work on flat bands is also significant, so excluding her leaves a credit question. The theory-plus-experiment trio is a natural prize structure.
assessment.maturity: Quite mature for its age: reproduced by many groups, with a rich body of follow-up work. The interpretation of superconductivity pairing is still unsettled.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is not agreed.
Sample variability (twist-angle disorder) limits reproducibility in detail.
Andrei and others (e.g. Dean/Kim groups on hBN moiré) make a three-person limit difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, including the Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site quantum-gas microscopy. This provides a new instrument for observing many-body physics directly. It is also a technique that others now use widely.
assessment.attribution: Greiner and Bloch observed the superfluid to Mott transition (2002) and later developed the microscopes; Esslinger realized the fermionic Mott insulator and many-body transport; Zoller and Cirac supplied the Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the simulation concept. Choosing the experimental trio leaves out the theory origin, which is a real allocation tension.
assessment.maturity: Mature: the technique is established worldwide and many results are reproduced. The promise of solving open problems (high-Tc phases) has been only partly met.
uncertainties: Whether the quantum simulation concept (Zoller, Cirac) should be credited ahead of an experimental trio.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and 2012 prize; some may think the key discoveries are not sharply defined.
Unclear whether simulators have yet answered a question not accessible by classical computing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single defect spins, especially NV centres in diamond, gave a room-temperature, nanoscale, magnetically sensitive probe used in materials, biology and quantum networks. It combines the quantum optics I know with real measurement impact, and the first single-spin optical detection was a clear experimental milestone.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup (single NV optical detection, 1997) is the central founding experimentalist; Awschalom (coherent control, SiC and other defects) and Lukin (nanoscale magnetometry proposals and demonstrations, with Walsworth) contributed to the sensing and quantum-technology branch. Allocation between founding discovery and the later sensing field is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a field and widely applied, with commercial sensors on the market. Some key applications are still evolving.
uncertainties: Lukin also appears on another candidate, and a single person cannot hold both positions in a clean way.
Walsworth's role and other NV pioneers (e.g. Jelezko) are not part of the three-person set, so credit is contested.
Whether sensing or quantum-information use is the prize-worthy core.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new classification of electronic matter, were verified experimentally with edge transport in HgTe and spectroscopy in Bi2Se3, and shape much of today's quantum materials research. Importance and originality are high.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theory (Z2 invariant, graphene QSH proposal), Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposed the HgTe route (not credited here), Molenkamp's group delivered the decisive transport experiment, and Hasan's ARPES work on 3D topological insulators is also a strong claim. A fair split among four credited names is difficult, and three names risk leaving out Hasan.
assessment.maturity: Mature: confirmed by many groups for more than a decade. Device or technology payoff is still limited, but the scientific impact is established.
uncertainties: Absence of Bernevig, Zhang and Hughes from the credited names limits an accurate attribution.
Choice between Molenkamp (2D) and Hasan (3D) for the experimental share.
Practical applications remain limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade turned single neutral atoms in tweezers into programmable arrays for quantum simulation and gate operations with hundreds of qubits. It is the most striking recent instrument-level progress in AMO, with experimental demonstrations clearly the leading element.
assessment.attribution: Browaeys demonstrated blockade between individual atoms; Lukin's group delivered large programmable arrays and quantum phases; Saffman did gate work and architecture; Zoller supplied the original blockade and gate proposals. Allocation between proposal and demonstration is not settled.
assessment.maturity: Maturing quickly but still developing; error rates and scalability claims are being tested and independent confirmations by several groups are in place. A prize may be a little early.
uncertainties: Premature relative to fault-tolerant demonstrations.
Lukin's name also appears on B039.
Role of theory (Zoller, Jaksch) versus experiment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution links the foundations of quantum mechanics to practical secure communication, with the BB84 protocol and entanglement-based E91 as the conceptual base and demonstrations over fiber and satellite links. As an experimentalist I value the real field demonstrations.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard created BB84; Ekert proposed the entanglement-based protocol, and Pan led the large-scale satellite and fibre experiments. The protocol inventors form the cleanest theory credit, but the experimental share is questionable if Pan is left out.
assessment.maturity: The concepts are very mature, but deployment and security of real devices remain open (side channels, rates), so impact beyond physics is still modest.
uncertainties: The 2022 Nobel for entanglement experiments already touched this area, which may reduce room for a new prize.
Omitting Pan leaves the experimental achievement unrecognized.
Practical security and rate limits lessen the maturity of the application.
